claims.text: Below 0.5 Tm, plastic deformation in equiatomic quaternary FCC alloys is primarily governed by dislocation glide.
Above 0.7 Tm, diffusion-controlled deformation becomes dominant.
Dominance of diffusion-controlled mechanisms at high temperature causes yield strength to become insensitive to strain rate.
Martensitic transformation or deformation twinning may compete with glide at cryogenic temperature or low stacking-fault energy.
Dislocation glide remains the dominant yielding mechanism in typical single-phase equiatomic FCC alloys.
The target initial state is a homogeneous, single-phase equiatomic quaternary FCC solid solution without secondary phases or precipitates.
The target alloy has a grain size of approximately 10–100 μm.
Intermediate-temperature tensile deformation produces dislocation cells and occasional deformation-induced nanotwins.
High-temperature deformation produces wavy or zigzag dislocation configurations associated with dislocation creep.
Dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding operate at high temperature.
Low-temperature work hardening results from dislocation interactions and occasional twinning.
Cryogenic deformation can induce an FCC-to-HCP martensitic transformation in low-stacking-fault-energy alloys, but this mechanism is secondary to glide.
Yield strength decreases as temperature increases.
Yield strength has weak strain-rate dependence above 0.7 Tm.
The strain-rate sensitivity parameter m approaches zero at high temperature when diffusion-controlled deformation dominates.
Cryogenic temperature significantly increases yield strength.
Deformation twinning at cryogenic temperature enhances work hardening.
Pure Ni and Cu have lower yield strength and different strain-rate sensitivity than equiatomic FCC alloys.
New diffraction peaks appearing below 2% strain regardless of strain rate would establish phase transformation as the dominant yielding mechanism.
Broadening of existing diffraction peaks without new phase peaks would establish dislocation glide as the dominant yielding mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis groups twinning with phase-transformation mechanisms and the mediator explicitly permits nanotwinning, but the falsification rule treats absence of new phase peaks as decisive evidence for glide. FCC deformation twins need not generate peaks from a new phase, so the proposed criterion could classify a twinning-mediated response as glide.
